question: In the early phase of the factory system, the East India Company permitted its employees to engage in 'private trade'. How did the Company historically define the boundary between official Company trade and private trade?
options: Private trade was strictly limited to commerce within Asia ('country trade'), while the import-export trade between India and Europe was reserved as an absolute monopoly of the Company.
Company trade was conducted only using precious bullion, whereas private trade had to be carried out strictly through barter.
Private trade was limited to luxury items like diamonds, musk, and pearls, while basic commodities like textiles and saltpetre were reserved for the Company.
Employees could trade in any commodity, but they had to pay a 50% commission to the Company on all private transactions.
explanation: Because the East India Company paid very low salaries to its factors and writers, it allowed them to carry on private trade. However, to protect its monopoly, the Company prohibited employees from sending goods to Europe (the 'home trade'). Instead, they were permitted to engage in local inter-Asian maritime commerce (the 'country trade'), which allowed many English factors to amass immense personal fortunes.
